startup.name: Compyle
startup.one_liner: The coding agent that actually collaborates with you
startup.description: Compyle is a less autonomous coding agent that asks before it acts. We're like Cursor or Claude Code - but you won't need to rewrite your codebase every time you use it for more than a small task. We built Compyle because we were frustrated with the direction other coding agents are headed. They're all racing to be more autonomous, running for hours without human input. This doesn't work for real production code. When agents run autonomously, they make countless small decisions that pile up in your codebase. Engineers lose ownership - they don't know what was implemented, can't effectively debug or maintain it, and struggle to build on top of it. The code becomes a black box, and they're forced to throw it away. Compyle keeps engineers in the driver's seat.

yc_acceptance.basis: Start from about 1 percent with a band of 0.6 to 2 percent (references/yc_acceptance.md). Up: two technical founders (technical founder in 74 percent of researched companies) with a distinct view that engineers lose ownership, and strong tailwinds in AI developer tools. Down: a very crowded space, takeover risk 5 in the closest analogs, and no traction stated. Net about 3 percent.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because coding agents are the most crowded AI category, and the pitch of asking before acting can be copied as a mode in Cursor or Claude Code. Without evidence that developers pay more for control, the interview would ask why the market wants less autonomy while everyone is racing to more.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2025 --industry B2B --calibration-only: seed 49% / 59% / 65%, cond 59% (n=126), months_to_seed 3 / 7 / 15 (n=74). Tag AI cohort: 50% / 61% / 67%. Developer Tools tag 2022-2025: seed 50% / 55% / 59%, cond 55% (n=29); series_a cond 38% (n=16).
anchors.adjustment_reason: The 59% anchor is for ever reaching seed. The forecast window is 13.4 months (from 2025-10-06 to 2026-11-17), and the cohort median time to seed is 7 months with a 75th percentile of 15 months, so about 60 to 70 percent of eventual seeds land inside it. That gives a window anchor near 0.37 to 0.42, and a round must also exceed $1M, which removes YC-deal-only cases. Set at 0.40, near the window anchor of about 0.40 for a 13 month window, with no lift for the hot coding agent theme. Coding agents are crowded and the YC analogs show mixed seed results, so the odds do not rank this company against others.

bands.rationale: Small post YC round of $1M to $3M, usually a pre-seed or angel led round that closes quickly. Cohort data for 2022 and later shows a 25th percentile near $2M, and a team this early often takes the first credible check.
Institutional seed of $3M to $6M, the middle of the 2022 and later table (median $3.2M to $3.5M, 75th percentile about $5M) lifted slightly because only rounds above $1M count here.
Hot sector seed of $6M to $12M. The 2026 winners test found 42 percent of confirmed raises here, but that sample leans to press covered rounds, so this band is held below that share.
Upside band above $12M, reached only with fast revenue or a standout founder story. Rare for a team of this size.

ladder.why_it_fails: Window: 13.4 months, to 2026-11-17. Window: 13.4 months, to 2026-11-17. Investors will ask why a two person team beats Cursor, Claude Code, Codex and Copilot, all of which can add a more collaborative mode with a setting. The thesis that less autonomy fits production code is a positioning, not a moat. Analogs such as Double and Freebuff show coding assistants with no post YC round, so a seed requires fast developer adoption and revenue, not just a clear point of view.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2025 --industry B2B --calibration-only: series_a cond 26% (n=74), months_to_series_a 22 / 29 / 38 (n=19). Tag AI: cond 23% (n=66).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Same 13.4 month window as the seed step. The 26% anchor is for ever reaching Series A after a seed, but the cohort 25th percentile for reaching Series A is 22 months from batch start, so only about 10 to 15 percent of eventual Series A rounds close inside a window this short. Set at 0.05 because coding tool companies need heavy usage and cost to reach Series A, and the cohort median to Series A is 29 months.

bands.rationale: Thin or bridge Series A near the 2022 and later 25th percentile of $11M, taken when growth is real but the story is narrow.
Typical Series A, anchored on the 2022 and later median of $14M to $15M and public medians of $17M.
Upside Series A of $20M or more for a category leader with fast ARR growth, as seen in the top AI cases.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series A inside 13 months would need explosive paid growth against better funded rivals and a compute bill that scales with usage. Developer tools in the cohort reached Series A on 38 percent of seeds but over a median of 30 months. Conductor reached a Series A and was acquired, an unusual speed. A team of two is unlikely to match that inside this window.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2025 --industry B2B --calibration-only: series_b cond 16% (n=19); calibration sample all years: 44% (n=126).
anchors.adjustment_reason: This step is for ever reaching a Series B given a Series A, with no time window, because recent cohorts are right censored. Set between the recent cohort figure of 16% (n=19, few years of follow up) and the all years figure of 44%, at 0.14 for a conservative read.

bands.rationale: Modest Series B near the 25th percentile of the 2022 and later table ($25M to $27M), likely a flat or small step up.
Typical Series B, median $37M to $40M with post money around $600M in the sparse data.
Upside Series B for a breakout. Few cohort examples, so the band is deliberately small.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series B requires beating the model vendors' own coding products, which are subsidized and tied to the best models. Margins depend on a vendor's model pricing, and no YC coding assistant analog in the data has reached a Series B. Enterprise code security needs also slow sales.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only: series_c cond 36% (n=55) across all years. The 2022 to 2025 B2B cohort has no Series C yet (n=3).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Anchor taken from the all years calibration sample because recent cohorts have not had time. Set at 0.25, about 0.7 times the anchor, since most Series B companies in this category face a very crowded late stage market.

bands.rationale: Series C near the 2022 and later 25th percentile ($35M to $50M), in a flat market.
Typical Series C or D, median $74M with post money about $1.2B.
Late stage breakout round. Very few researched cases, so this is a thin tail.

ladder.why_it_fails: Late stage rounds would need Compyle to be a leading coding tool. The leaders raise at valuations in the billions, and smaller coding tools are more often acquired, or hired out as a team, before they reach a Series C.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most paths end in a stall or small acquisition because model vendors bundle coding agents at subsidized prices and developers switch tools often. Compute cost per user can exceed revenue, and the founders' collaboration thesis may become a feature of the leaders.

killers.risk: Leading coding agents add a collaborative mode
killers.evidence: Cursor, Claude Code and Codex iterate monthly and already include plan and approval steps in their products.
killers.mitigation: Build workflow depth around specs and review that is hard to bolt on, and win a niche team.

killers.risk: Inference cost and model vendor pricing squeeze margins
killers.evidence: Model vendors subsidize heavy usage on their own subscriptions, which pressures third party tools that pay per token.
killers.mitigation: Use caching and smaller models for planning steps and price by seat with caps.

killers.risk: Demand for less autonomy is a niche view
killers.evidence: The market is racing toward autonomous agents and developers who want quality skew to the vendors with the best models.
killers.mitigation: Prove with teams that review burden falls and codebase health improves, and publish the numbers.

competition_now.name: Cursor
competition_now.what: AI code editor with agent features, large installed base.

competition_now.name: Claude Code and OpenAI Codex
competition_now.what: Terminal and cloud coding agents from the model vendors.

competition_now.name: GitHub Copilot
competition_now.what: Incumbent assistant inside the dominant code host.

technical_complexity.rationale: A planning and approval loop around existing models is within reach of two engineers in three months. The hard parts are context management on large codebases, evaluation of quality and reliable edits, and these depend on third party models whose vendors compete.

takeover_risk.rationale: The leaders ship features monthly and a more collaborative mode is a setting away. A rival needs about three months and has the distribution and incentive to keep developers in its product.

evidence.claim: AI coding tools are one of the most heavily funded categories, with very high valuations for leaders.
Developers reported that task level gains vary and that predictability and review burden are recurring complaints, which supports the control thesis.

roadmap.goal: Show developers who prefer the controlled workflow.
actions: Release a public beta to 200 developers and measure retention
Publish before and after on code review time
roadmap.proof: Weekly retention above 40 percent among beta users

roadmap.goal: Paid teams and a clear reason not to switch.
actions: Sell team plans to ten engineering orgs
Show a measure of codebase quality or ownership
roadmap.proof: $30K monthly recurring revenue and positive gross margin

roadmap.goal: A defensible position against model vendors.
actions: Build workflow depth the vendors will not copy quickly
roadmap.proof: $2M annual recurring revenue growing 15 percent a month

pros.point: Technical founders with a differentiated view
pros.evidence: The thesis that autonomous agents erode code ownership addresses a real complaint among developers.
Investors have valued AI coding companies very highly, so seed capital for a credible team is available.

brand.name: Compyle
brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Compyle" --era 2022+: invented or proper, 7 characters, 3 syllables
weaknesses: Misspelling of compile, easy to mistype
brand.rationale: Compyle is an invented word that signals code and compilation, in the style of developer tools such as Vercel, but its spelling invites typos. The effect is neutral because adoption turns on product quality.

narrative.headline: A thoughtful positioning in the most crowded AI category, where leaders can copy the idea in a quarter.
narrative.general_summary: Compyle is a coding agent that asks before it acts, aimed at teams that fear losing ownership of the code. The complaint is real and the founders are technical, but model vendors and Cursor ship monthly and a more collaborative mode is easy to add. Over a 13 month window the chance of a round above $1M is near the cohort window anchor, and a Series A is unlikely. The odds do not rank this company against others.

assumptions: Team of two with no disclosed traction as of 2025-10-06.
Funding figures for later rounds of leaders were ignored when dated after the as of date.

The seed probability is for a window of 13.4 months and a round above about $1M. It does not rank this company against others: in the 2026 winners test the average seed probability was 0.65 for companies that raised and 0.62 for companies confirmed to have raised nothing beyond the YC deal.
Series B and C plus steps are for ever reaching the round, not inside the window. Reaching a round years later is common for companies with paying customers.
Knowledge base coverage: calibration cohorts are 2022 to 2025 B2B (n=150 researched), with funding coverage partial for most, so known-only rates are biased low.
